summary: Defines an architecture for SIP peering, including its functional parts and interfaces. It also walks through the steps needed to set up a session between two SIP service provider domains. This informational document is part of the SPEERMINT working group's output.

eli5.summary: Imagine two phone companies who want their customers to call each other over the internet. This document draws the blueprint for the pieces they need and the steps to make a call work.

questions: how do sip service providers interconnect
what is a session border controller
what functions does the sbe perform
subtitle: How phone companies interconnect their SIP networks to call each other's customers.

tldr.problem: Phone companies that use SIP for calls need a way to interconnect their networks so customers can call people on other networks. There was no standard blueprint for how to do this.
tldr.mechanism: SPEERMINT defines the functional parts of a peering architecture: lookup and routing functions to find the destination network, signaling border elements to process the call setup, and data border elements to handle the voice stream.
tldr.outcome: The architecture enables Layer 5 SIP-level peering between service providers, providing a reference model that implementations can follow.

today: RFC 6406 is an Informational document that provides the reference architecture for SIP peering. It has not been obsoleted and remains the foundation for how SIP-based service providers implement interconnection today.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6406 defines a peering architecture for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and its functional components and interfaces. It addresses the Layer 5 signaling level, where two SIP Service Providers (SSPs) interconnect to enable calls between their customers. The architecture describes the components and steps needed to establish a multimedia session between two peering domains.

The document uses terminology from RFC 5486 and complements other SPEERMINT-related documents that define requirements and use cases. The focus is on the architectural blueprint rather than on specific security mechanisms or signaling details.
sections.eli5: Two phone companies want their customers to call each other through the internet. This is the blueprint for what pieces they need at the border and how they connect.

sections.title: Reference Architecture
sections.content:
The peering architecture consists of functional elements that sit on the administrative border between two SSP domains. On each side are a Signaling Path Border Element (SBE), which processes SIP messages, and a Data Path Border Element (DBE), which handles the media such as voice and video.

Within the SBE live three core functions. The Lookup Function (LUF) determines the target domain for a request by consulting services like ENUM (telephone number to SIP address translation). The Location Routing Function (LRF) discovers the address of the destination network's signaling point using DNS or other lookup mechanisms. The Signaling Function (SF) routes the actual SIP messages and can implement security policies and admission control.

The DBE performs media-related tasks such as transcoding (converting voice from one codec to another), media relaying, and media security. Both elements may exist in a single device called a Session Border Controller (SBC), or be distributed across multiple devices depending on the provider's network design.
sections.eli5: At the border between two phone networks sit pieces that do three jobs: look up where a call should go, find the address of the destination network, and then send the call request there. A separate piece handles the actual voice or video.

sections.title: Session Establishment Steps
sections.content:
To establish a call between users in two different SSP networks, a series of steps occur in order. First, the originating SSP uses the Lookup Function to determine which target SSP owns the dialed number. Second, the Location Routing Function finds the address of the target SSP's signaling point. Third, a SIP request is sent to that address. Fourth, media is exchanged between the user agents. Fifth, either party can end the call with a BYE message.

The originating SSP performs steps 1 through 4. The target SSP performs step 4, and both can perform step 5. If the call is redirected to a different target SSP, the sequence repeats from the beginning.
sections.eli5: To make a call: look up who owns the phone number, find that company's call server, send the call request there, start exchanging voice, and eventually hang up.

sections.title: Trusted Relationships and Security
sections.content:
Because peering occurs across administrative boundaries, establishing trust between the SSPs is essential. The document describes three approaches to securing signaling between peers. TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts and authenticates the connection; each SSP presents a certificate that the other verifies. The Signaling Function can verify the sender's identity header and confirm that the domain in the certificate matches the sender's domain.

IPsec is another option for protecting the link between signaling functions, though the RFC notes that additional specification is needed for practical deployment. Co-location is a deployment option where the SSPs place their signaling equipment in a shared, physically secure facility; in this case, messages may be sent unencrypted, though other access controls should still apply.

The receiving SSP must verify that incoming requests correspond to one of its own domains and may reject requests from unauthorized peers with a 403 Unsupported Peer response.
sections.eli5: Two phone companies need to trust each other. They can lock their connection with encryption, use special network protocols, or place their equipment in the same secure building. They also check that calls are from approved peers.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Peering requires that the interconnected SSPs operate in a common IP address space, which could be the public Internet or a private address space. If the originating and terminating networks use different address spaces, Network Address Translation (NAT) may be needed before traffic enters the peering interface. The only requirement is that all entities across the peering interface are reachable from each other.

The Data Path Border Element is responsible for media-related functions. An example is transcoding from the G.711 codec used by one SSP to the EvRC codec used by another. The DBE may also implement media relaying, privacy and encryption, and media security as defined in RFC 3711 (SRTP). These functions ensure that media streams are compatible between networks and properly protected.
sections.eli5: Two phone networks may not use the same IP addresses, so they may need a translator at the border. The voice data also needs to be converted if the networks use different formats, and it can be encrypted for privacy.
